answer: Providers and deployers of AI systems must take measures to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy of their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf [1]. When doing so, they must take into account technical knowledge, experience, education, training, the context of use, and the persons or groups on whom the systems are to be used [1].

Under the AI Act, prohibited AI practices include the placing on the market, putting into service, or use of an AI system that deploys subliminal techniques beyond a person’s consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques [1]. The objective or effect of these techniques must be to materially distort the behavior of a person or a group of persons by appreciably [1]. Additionally, AI systems used to detect the emotional state of individuals in workplace and education situations should be prohibited [2].

According to the AI Act, an 'AI system' is defined as a machine-based system designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy, which may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment and which, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers from the input it receives how to achieve them [2].

answer: An AI system is classified as high-risk if it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product covered by Union harmonization legislation and fulfills the required conditions [2]. Additionally, AI systems referred to in Annex III are considered to be high-risk [1], [5].

The risk-management system for high-risk AI systems should adopt the most appropriate risk-management measures in light of the state of the art in AI, and the provider must document and explain these choices [1]. It should consist of a continuous, iterative process planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle of the system [2]. This process aims to identify and mitigate relevant risks on health, safety, and fundamental rights [2]. Additionally, the risk-management system should be regularly reviewed and updated to ensure its continuing effectiveness, along with the justification and documentation of any changes [2].

High-risk AI systems that use techniques involving the training of AI models must be developed using training, validation, and testing data sets that meet specific quality criteria and are subject to data governance [1]. These data sets must be relevant, sufficiently representative, complete, and to the best extent possible free of errors in view of the intended purpose [5]. They must also possess the appropriate statistical properties, including regarding the persons or groups of persons for whom the system is intended to be used [5].

cited_pages: eu_ai_act_20 p.59 | eu_ai_act_20 p.20 | eu_ai_act_20 p.59
answer: High-risk AI systems must technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system [1, 2]. These logging capabilities must enable the recording of events relevant for identifying situations where the system may present a risk or undergo a substantial modification, facilitating post-market monitoring, and monitoring the operation of the system [1, 5]. Additionally, for high-risk AI systems referred to in point 1(a) of Annex III, the logging capabilities must record, at a minimum, the period of each use of the system, including the start and end date and time [5].

cited_pages: eu_ai_act_20 p.60 | eu_ai_act_20 p.21 | eu_ai_act_20 p.21
answer: High-risk AI systems must be designed and developed so that natural persons can effectively oversee them during their period of use [1]. Human oversight aims to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights that may emerge during use [1]. Appropriate human oversight measures should be identified by the provider before the system is put on the market or into service [4]. Furthermore, high-risk AI systems should include mechanisms to guide and inform the assigned natural person to make informed decisions on when and how to intervene [3].

cited_pages: eu_ai_act_20 p.25 | eu_ai_act_20 p.67 | eu_ai_act_20 p.23
answer: Deployers of high-risk AI systems must take appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure they use these systems in accordance with the accompanying instructions for use [2]. They play a critical role in protecting fundamental rights, complementing the obligations of the provider [1]. Furthermore, under specific conditions such as putting their name or trademark on the system, a deployer may be considered a provider and assume all relevant obligations [3].
The deployer of the high-risk AI system must carry out the fundamental rights impact assessment [1, 2].

answer: AI systems that generate or manipulate image, audio, or video content constituting a deep fake must clearly and distinguishably disclose that the content has been artificially created or manipulated by labelling the AI output accordingly and disclosing its artificial origin [1, 2]. In cases involving the rights and freedoms of third parties, this transparency obligation is limited to disclosing the existence of such generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display, enjoyment, or normal exploitation of the work, while maintaining its utility and quality [3].

In order for processing to be lawful, personal data should be processed based on the consent of the data subject or another legitimate basis laid down by Union or Member State law, either in the regulation or elsewhere [3]. Additionally, the processing of personal data strictly necessary for preventing fraud constitutes a legitimate interest of the data controller [1].

Yes, the data subject has the right to withdraw their consent at any time, and it must be as easy to withdraw consent as it is to give it [1, 4]. The withdrawal of consent does not affect the lawfulness of processing that was based on consent before its withdrawal [1, 4]. Regarding the conditions for consent, the request for consent must be presented in a manner that is clearly distinguishable from other matters, and it must be in an intelligible, easily accessible form using clear and plain language [1]. Furthermore, the data subject must be informed prior to giving consent [4]. When assessing if consent is freely given, utmost account must be taken of whether the performance of a contract or provision of a service is conditional on consent to process personal data that is not necessary for that performance [4].

Under the GDPR, the processing of a child's personal data in relation to information society services is lawful where the child is at least 16 years old [1]. However, Member States may provide by law for a lower age, provided that it is not below 13 years [4].

Under the right of access, the data subject has the right to obtain confirmation from the controller as to whether or not their personal data are being processed [1]. If that is the case, they get access to the personal data and information regarding the purposes of the processing, the categories of personal data concerned, and the recipients or categories of recipients to whom the data have been or will be disclosed [1].

A data subject has the right to erasure ('right to be forgotten') when the retention of the personal data infringes the GDPR or Union or Member State law to which the controller is subject [1]. Furthermore, this right applies when the personal data are no longer necessary in relation to the purposes for which they were collected or otherwise processed, or when the data subject has withdrawn consent or objects to the processing [1, 2].

The right to data portability allows a data subject to receive the personal data concerning them, which they have provided to a controller, in a structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format [3, 4]. It also includes the right to have the personal data transmitted directly from one controller to another, where technically feasible, provided the processing is carried out by automated means [4]. This right applies when the data was provided on the basis of consent or for the performance of a contract, but it does not apply to processing necessary for a task carried out in public duties [1, 4].

A data subject has the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning them or similarly significantly affects them [2]. Additionally, they have the right to obtain meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and envisaged consequences of such automated decision-making [4].

In the case of a personal data breach, the controller must notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it [1, 3]. This requirement applies unless the controller can demonstrate that the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons [1, 3]. Where the notification is not made within 72 hours, it must be accompanied by reasons for the delay [2].

A data protection impact assessment is required prior to processing in cases where processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons [3]. Specifically, it is required for a systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects based on automated processing, including profiling, that produces legal effects or significantly affects the person [4]. It is also required for large-scale processing of special categories of data, biometric data, or data on criminal convictions, as well as for the large-scale monitoring of publicly accessible areas, particularly using optic-electronic devices [1, 2]. Furthermore, it is required for operations where the competent supervisory authority considers the processing likely to result in a high risk because it prevents data subjects from exercising a right, using a service, or entering a contract, or because it is carried out systematically [1].

A data protection officer must be designated in any case where the processing is carried out by a public authority or body (except for courts acting in their judicial capacity) [4]. They must also be designated when the core activities of the controller or processor consist of processing operations that require regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale, or when required by State law [1, 4].

Under the GDPR, certain infringements are subject to administrative fines of up to 20,000,000 EUR, or up to 4% of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [4]. Additionally, infringements of other specified provisions are subject to administrative fines of up to 10,000,000 EUR, or up to 2% of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [5]. If a controller or processor infringes several provisions, the total amount of the fine shall not exceed the amount specified for the gravest infringement [5].
